label: Luck and help
rationale: Quick verdicts on how something went: lucky, unlucky, that helped, that did me good.
mixUps: un ga ii and un ga warui are one pair, so drill them in one frame (un ii ne! / un warui na). yaku ni tatsu is practical help with a task (not benri, handy); tame ni naru is something that does you good over time, like a talk, a book or an experience.

targets.trap: English 'lucky' is an adjective on the person. Japanese usually makes luck the subject, un ga ii (your luck is good), though rakkii! and tsuiteru are just as natural in casual speech. 'Good luck!' before a test or game is ganbatte, not anything with un.
partners: engi (engi ga ii: a good omen)
targets.use: Said when luck goes someone's way: un ii ne! (lucky you), with ga dropped. The past un yokatta (that was lucky) is just as common. Ii becomes yo- in its other forms, so it's never un iikatta.
targets.notes: Un ii ne (lucky you) sounds the same as un, ii ne (yeah, nice), so context decides. Kouun (幸運) is the written word.

example.romaji: ichiban mae no seki? un ii ne!

examplePolite.romaji: ichiban mae no seki desu ka? un ga ii desu ne!
examplePolite.ja: 一番前の席ですか？運がいいですね！

targets.trap: As with un ga ii, luck is the subject: un ga warui (my luck is bad). For your own bad day, tsuitenai is the more natural casual choice (kyou tsuitenai naa); un warukatta ne is the usual consolation.
partners: engi (engi ga warui: a bad omen)
targets.use: Said about your own bad luck (kyou un warui naa) or to console someone: un warukatta ne (that was just bad luck). Casual speech drops ga.
targets.notes: Fuun (不運) is the written word, and anrakkii is rare.

example.ja: 今日、ほんと運悪いなあ。
example.english: I'm having such bad luck today.

examplePolite.romaji: sore wa un ga warukatta desu ne.
examplePolite.ja: それは運が悪かったですね。

targets.trap: 'Useful' leads to benri, which means handy or convenient to use. yaku ni tatsu means it actually helped you with something, and it's the one for advice and information: advice that helped is yaku ni tatta, not benri datta.
targets.use: Said about advice, information, tools or people being of real use. You hear the past yaku ni tatta (that helped) most, then yaku ni tatenakute gomen (sorry I couldn't help) and the negative yaku ni tatanai (no use; harsh if said of a person).
targets.notes: tasukatta (you saved me) is the warmer thanks when someone helps you. To offer help: nanika yaku ni tateru koto attara itte ne. A talk, book or experience that does you good in the longer run is tame ni naru (tame ni naru hanashi), and to thank a senior for a talk, say benkyou ni narimashita.

example.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, sugoku yaku ni tatta yo.
example.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、すごく役に立ったよ。
example.english: That app you told me about the other day was really useful.

examplePolite.romaji: kono mae oshiete kureta apuri, hontou ni yaku ni tachimashita.
examplePolite.ja: この前教えてくれたアプリ、本当に役に立ちました。
examplePolite.english: The app you told me about the other day was really useful.

targets.verbSense: naru: become; here, turn out to be of benefit
partners: sankou (sankou ni naru: useful as a reference)
kusuri (ii kusuri ni naru: a setback that teaches you a lesson)
targets.use: Said about a book, show, talk or piece of advice you come away from knowing more: ano bangumi, tame ni naru yo. Ni is kept, and before a noun it's tame ni naru hanashi (a talk worth hearing). With a person, X no tame ni naranai means it does X no good.
targets.notes: Not the grammar -tame ni (in order to): here the phrase ends in naru, and tame means benefit. benkyou ni narimashita is the thank-you said on the spot; tame ni naru judges a book, show or advice as good for you; yaku ni tatsu says it was of practical use (a tool, a tip that helped).

example.romaji: ano hon, honto ni tame ni naru yo.
example.ja: あの本、ほんとにためになるよ。

examplePolite.romaji: ano hon wa hontou ni tame ni narimasu yo.
examplePolite.ja: あの本は本当にためになりますよ。

reviewPool.english: speak to, call out to; ask along
play games (video games, cards and the like)
not feel well, be under the weather (the safe phrase at work)
be in good shape, going well
feel sick (queasy or faint); feel put off
